Question: Are prisoners getting an education in jail?
Answer: Jails in the United States typically house inmates with charges awaiting trial and convicts serving less than a year. Realistically, there's not much demand for educational opportunities in the average municipal lockup. At the Salem/Roanoke County Jail where I was incarcerated, there WAS a walk-in library. We were fortunate in that regard, because many of the regional jails in our immediate vicinity (rural SW VA) had little more than a book storage closet and a trustee with a pushcart. There were no classes that I was made aware of. You could leave your cell and day room for rec/library time, visits to the commissary window, and prayer meeting. And that's about it. Ours was a work release pod so we DID get to put in a full eight hours five days a week. If we intended to learned anything while doing so, it was basically on us. Mostly, jail administration just wanted to see us serve our time and process out the other end. If we left jail an improved product, then nifty. But that was never the specific intent. The Big House is for learning. You wanna work on yourself then you better end up there. …because jail is a storage facility, not a community college.

Question: Is it a dress code rule in county jail or federal prison to wear socks to bed?

The only reasons I EVER removed my socks in county was — And that's it. Despite the CO’s wheeling in a janitorial cart once a day, and every con in the pod swabbing the day room floor, our individual cells (particularly the stainless steel toilet/sink combo), and the shower stall and additional open air communal head at the end of the second tier catwalk — despite all this — the surfaces in jail were never truly clean. Jails and prisons are veritable petri dishes for tinea pedis, protozoa, cold/flu viruses and your everyday run-of-the-mill despair. And in an environment where a relatively mundane illness can blossom into something life-threatening due to substandard healthcare, you do what you can to minimize contact. And if that means wearing socks and marginalizing bunkies who refuse to get with the program, then so be it. We called the few prisoners stupid enough to go barefoot in the pod “Jethros.” And it wasn't a term of endearment. Nobody wanted a Jethro for a cellmate. They usually ended up camping out on yoga mats under the corrugated steel stairway rather than getting a cellie. So the sock thing, like the courtesy flush, was a rule of our very own. And you broke it at your own peril.

Question: What if you could give up one of your parent's skills without missing it, which skill would you give up and why?
Answer: I've relinquished most of my dad's skill sets, not because I found them of no particular use, but because I never had his aptitude for either heroics or mathematics. My father was a self-taught civil engineer who became a certified land surveyor in the state of Virginia, despite never attending college. He was also an avid hunter and fisherman who would go with friends to the North Carolina shore on occasion for Gulf Stream charters. The captain of the fishing boat my dad hired that day was a likeable enough fellow. He liked my dad. He liked my dad's buddies. He liked the case of Budweiser and handle of Jack Daniels Old #7 they brought along with them in a Coleman cooler. And as the sun set that evening, miles from landfall, it became apparent to my father and his crew that their captain had been sneaking refreshments throughout the day, when they found him sprawled out across the bunk in the boats cabin, snoring and unresponsive. Before my father took his second certification exam, he employed the services of the elderly woman who tutored me in grade school math, to help him brush up on his Polaris. Even back then, civil engineers rarely relied on the stars to orient themselves, but my dad wanted to prepare for all possible examination scenarios. As it turned out, he wasn't required to know Polaris to pass that particular test. But on the boat that night, miles from port, it was clear skies and moonless. He started the motor, engaged the prop, and aimed the prow straight towards Nags Head. I miss my father. I miss his calm and self assurance. I wish I was capable of taking an unfortunate situation and turning into an opportunity for the sort of simple heroics that he was capable of. I long to see the stars to guide me home.

Question: What is the reason for serving steak mid-rare instead of fully cooked?
Answer: A medium rare steak IS “fully cooked.” Once a slab of beef is grilled to a uniformly grey interior, it's also uniformly dry and uniformly tough. That's the nature of beefsteak. If safety’s your concern, an interior temperature of 145 °F (62.8 °C) is the bottom threshold for done. Anything there and above is bacteria free. So get yourself a meat thermometer. I aquired my penchant for rare beef from my Dad. He was raised poor…never had steak as a kid…so ate his well-done as a young man until some friends invited him over for a candle lit prime rib dinner one night. It was revelatory. And it wasn't till he helped clean the dining room table and took the dishes to the florescent lighted kitchen that he could see the vivid pink drippings on the serving platter. That's not blood, by-the-way, but myoglobin tinted water, the same substance that makes chicken wings, legs and thighs dark rather than white. If you're going to eat meat then I personally don't see much point in being squeamish about something like that. People take their life into their own hands every time they eat a garden salad.

Question: What do inmates need to bring to jail/prison? What should they avoid bringing?
Answer: As a work release inmate, I was told to bring one change of clothes, a padlock with two keys (one of which went to the desk sargent), a windup alarm clock, wristwatch, and a pair of shower shoes. After I had showered, was sprayed with a delousing agent, and had blood drawn by a medic, I was handed bedding and toiletries, then walked up to the pod and assigned to a cell. The alarm clock went on a plastic chair by the bunk, the bedding went on the gym mat we were issued by way of a mattress, and everything else went on the floor under my pallet. And that's that. I was told exactly what I could and could not bring with me to jail because of my work release status. My advice is to not bring anything in with you that you don't want to end up stored in a property basket for the duration of your sentence. Because barring extenuating circumstances, it's not gonna make it up the elevator with you to your floor.
